sections: E.3. UMI →YAM Transfer: Embodiment Gaps and Ablations

blocks.text: Ablation 2: wrist-view alignment. We re-render the native UMI fisheye (≈180∘) as a virtual standard-FOV pinhole camera at the same optical center that imitates YAM’s 78 × 63∘wrist view (Tab. 16 and Fig. 43): a 202.96 px focal length at 320 × 240 (76.5 × 61.2∘), pitched about 27.1∘down, with rotation and focal length fitted in Isaac Sim on 112 same-scene UMI/YAM render pairs. On held-out pairs, the scene error is 8 px for objects closer than 30 cm and 11 px beyond, versus 74 and 94 px for the stereographic view, and the grasp zone is resolved at 12.5 rather than 6.9 px/cm for the raw fisheye. Identical maps back-fill the training data and run at deployment. We stress that this alignment is approximate. It matches the field of view and the viewing direction of YAM’s wrist camera, but not the lens, the stereo baseline, the offset of the optical center from the gripper, or the appearance of the arm and fingers in the frame, and the residual discrepancy is visible in Fig. 43. We compare three training views for the UMI wrist cameras: the stereographic view used in pretraining, the YAM-aligned view, and a random choice between the two on every training sample. Only the aligned view transfers on the two long-horizon tasks (Tab. 17). With the stereographic view, end-to-end success is 0% on both long-horizon tasks, and 46% of the items are sorted on Conveyor Belt Sorting and Tossing. The random mixture recovers 60% on tossing but still 0% on the long-horizon tasks, while the aligned view reaches 60%, 50%, and 86%. The progress scores tell a more specific story. They fall only moderately without alignment (96 to 79 on Toy Dumptruck Assembly, 86 to 76 on NIST Board Disassembly), so the policy still performs most steps. What it loses is the precision steps, in which the gripper must meet a screw hole or a nut within a few millimetres. A view mismatch moves the grasp zone in the image and changes its pixel scale (12.5 versus 6.9 px/cm), which corrupts exactly the image-to-action mapping those steps depend on, while leaving coarse transport intact. The random mixture helps only on tossing (60% versus 46%), where coarse transport suffices, and not on the precision steps, because it asks the policy to be invariant to a viewpoint change that is informative for those steps. The policy averages over two geometries and is sharp in neither. We draw two conclusions. First, the video model absorbs the appearance gap, since human arms and a handheld gripper in training versus robot arms in deployment do not prevent transfer, but it does not absorb a geometric gap. Second, the geometry need only be roughly matched: coarse agreement in field of view and viewing direction is sufficient to recover most of the transfer, which makes the method practical for new target robots whose wrist cameras are known only from a datasheet.
blocks.section: E.3. UMI →YAM Transfer: Embodiment Gaps and Ablations

blocks.text: Ablation 3: amount of UMI data. The UMI demonstrations are the only source of the target task, so their number bounds how much task evidence post-training can draw on. We shrink each cohort to about half and a quarter of its episodes at a fixed 0.6 : 0.4 UMI : YAM sampling ratio (Tab. 17). The three tasks degrade very differently. Conveyor Belt Sorting and Tossing is nearly flat (86%, 84%, 70%): it is a short-horizon dynamic skill with one decisive event, and 20 episodes already cover it. Toy Dumptruck Assembly degrades gradually in end-to-end success (60%, 30%, 10%) while its progress score stays high (96, 92, 81), the signature of a long horizon in which small per-step losses compound multiplicatively. Notably, the policy trained on only 20 demonstrations still completes the full four-stage assembly end to end in 1 of 10 trials and 81% of its individual steps, on a robot that has never been teleoperated for the task. NIST Board Disassembly collapses at the first halving (50% to 0%), and the substage table shows why: the nut subtask goes from 5 of 10 to 0 of 10 while the other four subtasks barely move. The data requirement of a task is therefore set not by its length but by its hardest subskill, the one with the least support in both the pretraining and the co-training data. That subskill is the first to disappear as demonstrations are removed, and in a sequential task its loss zeroes the end-to-end rate. In practice, 41 to 75 handheld demonstrations sufficed for every task here, and half of that sufficed whenever the task contained no such rare subskill.
blocks.section: E.3. UMI →YAM Transfer: Embodiment Gaps and Ablations

blocks.text: Ablation 4: UMI-10K in pretraining. The main result (Tab. 4) already shows that starting from a checkpoint pretrained without UMI data reduces transfer success to 20% and 0% on the long-horizon tasks and the share of conveyor items sorted to 34%. We repeat the row in Tab. 17 and examine what pretraining contributes. Both models see the same post-training data and the same number of steps, so the difference lies entirely in what the pretrained weights already encode. The checkpoint without UMI also differs in pretraining length, robot mixture, and small model details (Sec. E.2), so not all of the gap need come from UMI data. We identify two contributions. First, with UMI-10 data in pretraining, UMI’s observation domain, a handheld gripper and human arms seen through fisheye wrist views, is already in-distribution for the video backbone, so post-training does not have to learn to see the demonstrations. Second, and more important for transfer, pretraining on UMI alongside YAM and the other robot corpora aligns UMI’s actions with the other embodiments inside the shared transformer: the model has already learned that a UMI grasp and a YAM grasp are the same event. Post-training then only needs to attach task evidence to an alignment that exists, whereas without UMI in pretraining the same 41 to 75 episodes must simultaneously teach the observation domain, bind it to YAM’s action semantics, and teach the task. The few-shot budget is spent on the embodiment rather than on the task. The progress scores are consistent with this reading. Without UMI pretraining the policy still performs most coarse steps (84 and 65), so it does learn the task structure. It fails at the precision steps, where an imprecise embodiment alignment turns into a missed hole or a dropped part. UMI data in cross-embodiment pretraining are thus not a convenience but the mechanism that makes a few dozen demonstrations sufficient.
